text: Trauma is a major cause of disease. Skin and subcutaneous injuries can cause local infection with slow healing if not treated: cut the hair around the wound and wash with water and a brush to create a dirt-free area, clean daily with water and soap to remove discharge, and inject a long-acting antibiotic if the wound is deep. Microbes can also enter the body and cause general infection through animal bites (in Cambodia, farmers should be aware of rabies risk from dog bites), poor technique (e.g. abscesses after injection, teeth clipping, or tail docking done improperly), or wounds where microbes such as Streptococcus or tetanus invade through breaks in skin or mucous membranes. Ongoing suffering — such as lameness (painful joints/feet reducing movement to eat/drink) or eye injuries (redness, discharge, possible foreign body or corneal damage, often leaving the animal immobile in shade) — reduces feed and water intake within days and weakens the animal, making it more vulnerable to other disease; pain-relieving medicines (paracetamol, phenylbutazone, analgine) support recovery. Some injuries impair function permanently: a broken leg generally leads to slaughter; a damaged vulva can cause infertility by preventing mating; wounded teats prevent normal milk removal and cause insufficient milking.
